# Part 3: Integration Engineering

## 3.1 Choosing the integration mechanism

An architect who cannot read the wire format cannot review the design. The model is one participant in a distributed system, and every failure that reaches a user travels through the same substrate every other enterprise integration travels through: an HTTP request, a schema, a token, a retry, a log line and a database. This part is that substrate, at the depth needed to challenge an implementation rather than write one.

The governing asymmetry: **the architect does not need to build these things and does need to be able to reject them.** Reading is the skill. Every section below is organized around what a bad version looks like, because that is the form the work takes.

The first decision is the connection mechanism itself. Three mechanisms move a capability across a boundary, a fourth moves a procedure, and one selection rule covers all four.

### MCP: agent to tools

**MCP** is a standard originated by Anthropic for exposing capabilities to models. A server publishes three things.

| Primitive | What it is | Who decides to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tools** | Actions the model can invoke | The **model**, reactively, mid-task |
| **Resources** | Read-only data the application can fetch | The **application**, proactively. No model decision involved |
| **Prompts** | Pre-written instructions the maintainer has tested | Either |

The consequence that matters is about ownership: **the team that knows the service best maintains one integration for everyone**, instead of every application maintaining its own. In *Building Effective Agents* Anthropic frames MCP as one way to implement the augmented LLM's augmentations.

Choose it when: the capability will be used by more than one client or agent; you want discoverability rather than hard-wiring; the service owner can maintain it; you want tools, readable data and prompts in one package. For standard third-party systems, prefer an existing server to building one.

**The deployment shape is the transport question, remote versus local, and it is a governance question as much as a technical one.** A **local server** runs on the caller's own machine or runtime and inherits that machine's identity, network egress and logging. In practice that means no central audit trail and no per-request attribution: the call is made by whoever is signed in to that machine, from whatever network it sits on, and the only record of it is local. A **remote server** is reached over the network, so it can carry a real service identity, sit behind the gateway, log centrally and be revoked in one place. The cost is that it stops being a convenience and becomes an operated product, with an owner, a service level and a deployment story. The rule follows from the asymmetry: **anything that reads or changes regulated data is a remote server behind the gateway**, and local servers are for developer convenience over non-regulated material. The identity questions this opens are 3.5 and the audit questions are 3.9.

**MCP does not replace tool use; it redistributes it.** Tools behave identically. What changes is who authors and maintains them.

### Direct API or CLI: the simple case

Calling the service the ordinary way from inside your application. Choose it when: one application consumes it; latency is critical and an extra hop is unwelcome; a mature client library exists; the interaction is narrow enough that a protocol layer is overhead. Fewer moving parts, less to operate.

### Agent-to-agent: agent to peer agent

Agent-to-agent connection means **A2A (Agent2Agent)**, a protocol originated by Google and now a Linux Foundation standard. Its release history, its signed-agent-card milestone and its adoption headcount are perishable and sit in Appendix I with the date they were verified. Three core concepts carry it.

| Concept | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Agent Cards** | The discovery mechanism. Each agent publishes a machine-readable document describing its name, capabilities, supported input and output types and authentication requirements. Analogous to a service descriptor |
| **Tasks** | The unit of work, with a lifecycle of eight states. Two are interrupted states, **input-required** and **auth-required**, and four are terminal, **completed**, **canceled**, **rejected** and **failed**, with **submitted** and **working** in between. A task that reaches a terminal state cannot restart, so a refinement is a new task inside the same context |
| **Messages and Artifacts** | Messages are the exchange during a task; artifacts are the deliverables the remote agent produces |

The distinction to hold: **MCP is the vertical connection**, an agent reaching into its own toolbox. **A2A is the horizontal connection**, one agent reaching out to a peer it does not control and does not need to understand internally. They are complementary layers, not competitors, and production multi-agent systems commonly use both: A2A across organizational or vendor boundaries, MCP wiring each agent to its own tools and data.

Choose A2A when: the work genuinely requires the other side's autonomy and its own capabilities; the two systems are owned by different teams or vendors; what should cross the boundary is a task with a goal rather than a parameterized call; and neither side should know the other's internals.

### Skills: a procedure as a deployed asset

The three mechanisms above move a *capability* across a boundary. A **Skill** moves a *procedure*, and it belongs in this decision rather than only in the prompting one (2.7) because it has a request-time surface, a publication surface and a runtime dependency, which is what makes it an integration mechanism rather than a packaging convention.

| Surface | What it is | What it implies for the architect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Attachment** | A Skill is attached to a request through the **`container.skills`** parameter | The procedure travels with the call rather than being resident in the prompt, so it is selected per request and is visible in the request record |
| **Publication and versioning** | Skills are published and versioned through the **`/v1/skills`** endpoint and managed under version control like any other deployed asset | Versioning, approval and rollback are available at the platform layer rather than being reimplemented per team. This is what a prompt library cannot offer |
| **Execution** | Skills require the **Code Execution Tool** to run | The mechanism carries a **sandboxed execution environment dependency**, which is a security review, a network egress question and an operational surface, not a configuration flag |

**The third row is the one that changes the decision.** A Skill is not a lighter-weight alternative to MCP. It brings an execution sandbox into the deployment, and in a regulated environment that sandbox is reviewed on the same terms as any other compute the system runs. An architect who reaches for Skills because they look like packaging has quietly added a runtime.

Choose it when: the same procedure runs repeatedly and identically; it must be distributed across teams or products; it needs versioning, approval and rollback as one governed artifact; and the sandboxed execution dependency is acceptable in the target environment. Where the procedure is a *tool surface* that several clients must reach, MCP remains the mechanism. **The two are weighed against each other, not layered by default.**

### The selection rule

**Prefer the simplest mechanism that satisfies the reuse and ownership requirements.**

| Situation | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| One application, one service, narrow interaction | **Direct API or CLI** |
| Multiple consumers, or a capability surface someone else should own | **MCP** |
| Two autonomous systems delegating goals across an organizational boundary | **A2A** |
| One repeatable procedure that must be versioned and distributed, where a sandboxed runtime is acceptable | **Skill** |

Two supporting points recur. Description quality decides adoption: a thinly described exposed tool loses to a familiar built-in capability even when it is better, and the fix is a better description. And resources reduce exploratory calls, because a catalog of what exists lets the model see the landscape without spending calls to discover it.

One vocabulary note. **Progressive discovery** and Anthropic's **just-in-time context** are the same idea under two names; recognize both. **Tool search** is an instance of the same principle, which connects this decision to the capability discipline of the next section.

### The five layers a governing constraint decides

The mechanism selection above is the first decision and not the whole of it. **An enterprise integration is five layers, and in a regulated deployment the constraint decides all five before the engineering preference gets a vote.** Reading the layers in this order is what stops a design being rebuilt after its first legal or security review.

| Layer | The architectural decision | What breaks when it is wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Compliance and regulated-industry constraints** | Which delivery routes and entry points survive the governing constraint. Business associate agreement coverage, FedRAMP authorization, data-residency pinning and approved-vendor lists each eliminate options before the rest of the design begins | The integration is built on a route that fails the next legal or security review. The cost of redesign is the time already invested plus a new architecture from scratch |
| **Identity and single sign-on** | Where the user identity boundary sits relative to the integration point. Who is the user in the context of a model call, and how does that identity get passed into the prompt safely | Without correct identity the model cannot scope its responses to what the user is authorized to see. Identity passed as a raw field in the user message is manipulable. Server-side injection removes that risk |
| **Authorization and policy** | Which capabilities this user or role has, and which data they may reach. The authorization model governing the existing systems has to govern the model layer as well | An integration that bypasses the underlying authorization model gives users access to data they are not entitled to, through a path that was never designed to enforce the access policy |
| **Data handling and personally identifiable information** | What data enters the context window. Sensitive fields passed in the user message or system prompt become part of the request, and any logging the application layer performs will capture them | A personally identifiable field passed directly in the user message appears in plaintext in the application's request logs. In a regulated industry that surfaces in the next audit rather than the next deployment |
| **Observability and audit logging** | What you need to be able to reconstruct, and what questions you will have to answer after an incident. Those answers determine what is logged, at what depth and for how long | An unlogged data path is invisible. When something goes wrong on it there is no evidence to reconstruct what happened, and building observability after the first incident always costs more than building it before |

**Reference identifiers are the practical instrument at the data-handling layer.** Account numbers and claim numbers are often needed for routing and not for the language task itself. Where a reference identifier is enough, passing the full data field exposes it to every request log the application layer performs without adding any capability.

### ⚠ The constraint-to-integration matrix

The following maps five common governing constraints across the layers above, with identity and authorization sharing the "Who it trusts" column because in practice one determination settles both. **It is a starting frame for the conversation with counsel and the security owner, not a determination.** Route eligibility, authorization scope and residency support are product facts that move, and every row here should be re-verified against current vendor documentation before it is relied on in a design.

| Constraint | Where it runs | How it connects | Who it trusts | What it handles | What it logs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Legal professional privilege** | Behind the firm's own application, through a firm-approved gateway that logs every request | The gateway sits between the user and the model, holds the API key, enforces who can access what and produces an audit log the firm owns | Users authenticate through single sign-on. Identity and permissions are assigned server side and cannot be claimed by the user | All privileged content flows through the gateway, which serves as the official record | Every request and response, retained according to firm policy |
| **Protected health information** | On a configuration covered by a business associate agreement. The agreement must cover the specific configuration in use, not the provider in general | The cloud provider mediates the integration where a cloud route is used | Users verified through the partner's authentication system. Access limited to the minimum necessary | Stripped to what the task requires before the call. Reference identifiers in place of full data fields where possible | Request, model version, user identity and data scope, retained to the applicable requirement |
| **Data residency under European rules** | Execution confined to an approved region, achieved through a cloud route or a residency-pinned configuration | The execution region is locked at the integration layer and checked on every request | Users verified within the approved data region | Personal data processed only within the pinned region. Cross-border movement requires a documented basis | Who accessed what data, the lawful basis for processing it and when it will be deleted |
| **Government and authorization programs** | On a cloud configuration holding the required authorization at the correct impact level | The architecture is limited to the specific cloud and configuration carrying the authorization. Nothing outside that boundary is allowed | Users authenticate through the agency's approved identity provider. Access controlled by the agency's role and policy layer | Handled according to the agency's classification rules. Controlled unclassified information stays inside the authorized boundary | To the agency's continuous monitoring requirements |
| **Internal data-residency policy** | On the cloud provider the organization has already approved. The right route is the one the chief information officer has cleared, regardless of convenience | Constrained by what procurement has approved, regardless of engineering preference | Users sign in through the organization's standard single sign-on. Roles assigned by existing policy | Per the existing classification scheme. The model layer inherits existing controls and does not introduce new ones | Into the existing logging infrastructure rather than a separate system |

Four specifics worth carrying, each of them perishable and each collected in Appendix I with its verification date.

**Residency and the transfer question are not the same question.** European data protection law does not require European residency as such, because cross-border transfers are lawful with a valid transfer mechanism. Where a deployment nonetheless carries a residency requirement, whether from a regulator, a customer contract or internal policy, a cloud route is the instrument rather than a request parameter. The `inference_geo` parameter pins United States inference and does not offer European pinning.

**The data processing agreement sits in a different place depending on the route.** On the direct API it is with Anthropic. On a cloud route the terms are inherited from the cloud contract, which means the party you would notify, and the party a regulator would look to, changes with the route.

**Authorization is configuration-specific, not vendor-specific.** A vendor holding an authorization on one configuration does not extend it to another, and an enterprise agreement on a direct API path is not a substitute for a route that carries the authorization itself.

**A residency capability announced but not shipped is not a design input.** Where a roadmap entry is the basis for a residency commitment, verify current availability before committing the route, and note the deployment's fallback if the date moves.

## 3.2 Capability discipline: privilege and scale

Capability problems in agent systems come in two distinct kinds with two different correct answers, and conflating them produces the wrong remedy.

| Problem | What goes wrong | The correct answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Excess privilege** | The agent holds capability its role does not need. Attack surface, misuse, injection leverage | **Remove the capability.** Security problem, security answer |
| **Excess scale** | The agent legitimately needs a large catalog. Context consumed, selection accuracy degraded | **Defer the definitions** with tool search. Context problem, context answer |

The distinguishing question is simple: **does the role need this capability at all?** If no, remove it, and no amount of clever loading fixes the security exposure. If yes, and there are simply many of them, removal is not available and the answer is a loading strategy.

### Problem one: excess privilege

Every capability held is a capability that can be misused, by the model erring, by a user manipulating it or by injected content in a document the agent reads. Anthropic's injection guidance makes the security framing explicit: apply least privilege so that **a successful injection can do minimal damage**, do not give Claude access to secrets it does not need, run tools in sandboxed environments and scope permissions as narrowly as possible.

The review method, one question per tool:

| Finding | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Not needed at all | **Remove it** |
| Needed in narrow form only | Replace the broad tool with a scoped one. A wide-open fetch-any-URL becomes a load-approved-document that validates its target |
| Needed occasionally by a role outside its specialty | Give a scoped version of that one capability, not the whole toolbox |
| Functionally overlapping with another tool | Rewrite descriptions to eliminate overlap, or consolidate |

The sharpest judgment in this area: logging and confirmation prompts are **detective and compensating controls** and do not shrink the attack surface. Removal does. A design that offers to watch, log, confirm, warn or gate excess capability instead of removing it has not addressed it.

### Problem two: excess scale, and the numbers

Anthropic quantifies this, which turns a judgment call into a threshold.

- **Tool selection accuracy degrades beyond roughly 30 to 50 tools loaded at once.**
- **50 tools consume roughly 10,000 to 20,000 tokens** in definitions alone.
- **A typical five-server setup** (GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, Splunk) **can consume around 55,000 tokens in definitions before Claude does any work.**

And the qualitative test, which is the best line in the documentation: **if a human engineer cannot definitively say which tool should be used in a given situation, an AI agent cannot be expected to do better.**

**The answer at scale is the tool search tool.** Rather than loading every definition up front, you provide all definitions and mark the ones that should not load with `defer_loading: true`, keeping at least one non-deferred tool, normally tool search itself. Claude's context initially contains only tool search and any non-deferred tools. When Claude needs a capability it does not have, it searches the catalog, which is matched against **tool names, descriptions, argument names and argument descriptions**, and the API returns matching tools as references, **up to five by default**, automatically expanded into full definitions and available for subsequent turns.

**The trade-off runs in both directions.** Tool search costs one extra round trip the first time a tool is discovered, offset by smaller context on every turn. Anthropic states the boundary: **with fewer than about ten tools, loading everything up front is typically faster.** So tool search is not a free improvement, and recommending it for a small toolset is over-engineering.

**Two variants exist and they take different queries.** The regex variant has Claude write a pattern; the BM25 variant takes a natural-language query. The choice affects how tool names and descriptions should be written, which is a further reason the namespacing rule below is not cosmetic.

**Model support is a published list rather than a generation rule.** Verified 2026-08-11: the compatibility table names Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5, and states that Opus 4.1 and earlier do not support it. **Sonnet 5 was not on that list at the verification date**, which is the reason to read the table rather than assume a newer model inherits the capability. The list, its date and the route-specific qualifications are in Appendix I.

### Tool definition quality

The description is the selection mechanism, so it is a design artifact. The specific guidance:

- **Aim for at least three to four sentences per tool description**, more if the tool is complex. Cover what the tool does, when to use it, what data it returns, what each parameter means and any important caveats or limitations, including what the tool does **not** return.
- **Use meaningful namespacing.** Where tools span multiple services, prefix with the service: `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`. This makes selection unambiguous as the library grows and is **especially important when using tool search**, since search matches on names.
- **Return only high-signal information.** Use semantic, stable identifiers such as slugs or UUIDs rather than opaque internal references, and include only the fields Claude needs to reason about its next step. Bloated responses waste context and make extraction harder.
- **Consolidate related operations into fewer tools.**
- For complex or format-sensitive inputs, provide schema-validated **input examples** alongside the description.
- Anthropic reports spending **more time optimizing tool definitions than the overall prompt** when building their own coding agent.

Plus the interface-design guidance from *Building Effective Agents*: give the model enough tokens to think before it writes itself into a corner; keep formats close to what appears naturally in text on the internet; avoid formatting overhead such as counting lines or escaping strings; and design the agent-computer interface with as much care as a human-computer interface. The worked example: a tool using relative file paths broke once the agent moved out of the root directory, and requiring absolute paths fixed it completely. Design the interface so the mistake is impossible.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question.** These tool servers are application programming interfaces, and the organization already governs those. Who is on call for one, and what happens to its dependent agents when it is down or its contract changes.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defining an agent's tool set | Least privilege review and periodic recertification of every granted capability | Tool privilege register with recertification dates. Security owner |
| Placing the authorization enforcement point | Evidence that it sits outside the model and cannot be bypassed | Authorization design with test evidence. Security architect |
| Integrating a peer agent across an organizational boundary | Liability for actions taken by an agent the organization does not control | Inter-company agreement with liability and audit terms. Legal |

**What this costs the organization.** Least privilege asserted once at design time decays as scopes widen under delivery pressure, and nothing here recurs. The cost people forget is the tool server as an operated product: an owner, a service level, an on-call rota, a versioned contract and a deprecation notice period, all attached to something the design treats as a configuration entry.

**The executive translation.** We are exposing existing systems to a new kind of client, so the same access controls, recertification and change discipline apply, and the model is never the control.
