## 3.3 The API surface

### Resource modeling

An **API resource** is a noun the enterprise already recognizes, exposed at a stable address, with a stable identifier. Three tests decide whether a proposed resource is real.

| Test | Passing looks like | Failing looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Does it have an identity that outlives a request?** | `/contracts/{id}` | `/searchContractsAndSummarize` |
| **Would a business person name it?** | contract, claim, matter, invoice | payload, record, item, object |
| **Can it be fetched, listed and changed independently?** | `GET /contracts/{id}`, `PATCH /contracts/{id}` | one endpoint that returns everything |

The recurring defect is the **verb endpoint**: an address that names an action rather than a thing. Verb endpoints do not version, cache, paginate or authorize by resource, and they accumulate one per use case until nobody can enumerate the surface. When an agent is the consumer the tool catalog inherits the endpoint catalog, so capability bloat follows directly from resource modeling failure.

**Decision rule: if the endpoint name contains a verb other than the HTTP method, the resource has not been modeled yet.**

The counter-pressure: a well modeled API with forty endpoints becomes a bad tool catalog with forty tools. The resolution is a **tool facade**, where each tool is a coarse task-level operation composed of several resource calls. The API is modeled for correctness and the tool surface for selection accuracy, and treating them as one artifact is the most common integration design error in agent systems.

### Tools you do not have to build

Before modeling a resource or writing a facade, check whether the capability already exists as a supplied tool. A published tool costs no build, no maintenance and no schema design, and the reason to know the set is that teams routinely build a worse version of something already available. The set divides on one line that matters architecturally more than the capability list does.

**Server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure. Client tools run on yours.**

| Class | What it means | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Server tools** | Anthropic publishes the schema *and* executes the call. Your application writes no handler and receives the result already computed. Several carry usage-based charges on top of tokens | Web search, web fetch, code execution in a sandboxed container, tool search, the advisor tool that lets a faster model consult a stronger one mid-generation, and the MCP connector for reaching a remote server without running an MCP client |
| **Anthropic-schema client tools** | Anthropic publishes the schema; your application executes every call. You own the runtime, the sandbox and the blast radius, and you pay only ordinary token pricing | Bash in a persistent session, text editor, computer use, and the memory tool that reads and writes files you control |
| **The Files API** | Not a tool but the adjacent mechanism: upload a file once and reference it across requests rather than re-sending its contents | Document workloads where the same source is used repeatedly, which is also a cost decision |

⌂ **The server-and-client line is a data-flow decision wearing a convenience label.** A server tool means content leaves your boundary to be processed on Anthropic's infrastructure, and for web search and web fetch it also means the system reaches the public internet from there rather than from your network. Both facts belong in the data-flow diagram, in the residency assessment (6.8) and in the vendor record, and neither is visible in the code, which is a single line enabling the tool. The corresponding client tool moves the execution back inside your boundary at the price of building and governing the sandbox yourself. That is a real trade and it should be made deliberately once, at the architecture, rather than repeatedly and invisibly by whoever adds the tool.

⧉ **Two of these carry an egress path that a security review will ask about and a design document usually omits.** Web fetch retrieves content the system did not choose, which makes every fetched page untrusted input under 4.4, and code execution runs generated code, which is a capability the risk tier (4.2) has to have contemplated. Neither is an argument against using them. Both are an argument for naming them in the architecture rather than discovering them in an incident review.

**The selection question is the ordinary one.** Does a supplied tool do this? If yes, use it and record what it implies for data flow. If it nearly does, prefer configuring it over rebuilding it. Only when the capability is genuinely specific to your systems does the facade in this section become the answer, and at that point the tool count discipline of 3.2 applies to the supplied tools too, since they occupy the same selection budget as the ones you wrote.

### Verbs and idempotency

**Idempotency** is the property that performing an operation twice leaves the system in the same state as performing it once. It is the single most important property in AI integration, because retries are unavoidable and agents retry on their own initiative as well as through your retry code.

| Method | Idempotent | Safe (no state change) | Retry without thought |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `HEAD` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `PUT` | Yes | No | Yes, if truly a full replace |
| `DELETE` | Yes | No | Yes, second call returns 404 or 204 |
| `PATCH` | **Not guaranteed** | No | **No.** Depends on the patch semantics |
| `POST` | **No** | No | **No.** Requires an idempotency key |

The mechanism that makes `POST` safe is an **idempotency key**: a client-generated unique value sent as a header, which the server stores alongside the result of the first successful execution and replays for any subsequent request carrying the same key. Three properties make an implementation correct rather than decorative.

1. The key is generated by the **caller** at the point the intent is formed, not at the point the HTTP call is made, so that a caller-side retry reuses it.
2. The server stores the key **before** performing the side effect, not after, so that a crash mid-operation does not permit a second execution.
3. The stored record has a **retention window** longer than the maximum retry horizon, and a documented behavior when the same key arrives with a different request body, which must be an error and not a silent overwrite.

**Decision rule: any tool that an agent can call which changes state outside your process must either be idempotent by construction or carry an idempotency key, and there is no third option.**

### Status codes that matter

Most status code lists are trivia. Six distinctions carry real design consequence in AI integration.

| Code | Means | What the integration must do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **400** | The request is malformed. It is not parseable or violates the syntactic contract | Do not retry. Fix the caller. In agent systems this usually means the model produced a tool argument the schema rejects, so the correct response is to return the validation error to the model as a tool result and let it repair |
| **422** | The request parsed and the schema matched, but the content is semantically invalid | Do not retry unchanged. This is a **business rule** rejection and it should carry a machine-readable reason code, because the model or the workflow must branch on it |
| **401** | Not authenticated. The system does not know who you are, or the token is expired or malformed | Refresh the credential once, then fail. Never retry blindly, since a loop against an authentication endpoint is how accounts get locked |
| **403** | Authenticated and not permitted | **Never retry.** A retry on 403 is a defect. Surface it as a permission outcome, not an error, because it is often the correct and expected answer |
| **429** | Rate limited. You exceeded a quota you were told about | Retry with backoff, honoring `Retry-After` when present. Feed the signal to the gateway so that concurrency is reduced rather than merely delayed |
| **529** | The upstream service is overloaded. Not your quota, their capacity | Retry with backoff and jitter, and consider failover. This is the code most commonly conflated with 429 and the two demand different responses: 429 says slow yourself down, 529 says the other side is in trouble |

400 versus 422 maps onto the two ways a model produces a bad tool call. A **shape error**, a disallowed or missing field, is a 400 and is repairable by returning the error text. A **content error**, well formed arguments referring to something that cannot be acted on, is a 422 and often is not repairable by the model at all, because it cannot know the account is closed. Returning 400 for both trains the loop to retry what it can never fix.

401 versus 403 is the one auditors ask about. **401 is an authentication outcome and 403 is an authorization outcome**, and a system that confuses them has an access log that cannot distinguish an identity failure from an entitlement failure.

**Decision rule: retry 429 and 529 with backoff, refresh once on 401, never retry 400, 403 or 422.**

### Pagination and filtering

Three pagination styles, with one correct default.

| Style | Mechanism | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Offset** | `?limit=50&offset=200` | The underlying set changes between pages, producing skipped and duplicated rows. Degrades badly at depth because the database still scans the skipped rows |
| **Cursor (keyset)** | `?limit=50&after=<opaque>` | Requires a stable sort key. Cannot jump to page 40 |
| **Token** | Server-issued continuation token, opaque and expiring | Token expiry mid-iteration must be handled |

**Decision rule: use cursor pagination for anything an agent iterates, because offset pagination silently produces duplicate and missing records under concurrent writes and an agent has no way to notice.**

A human notices a repeated row. An agent summing a column does not. **Pagination defects in agent tool results present as arithmetic errors, not as pagination errors,** which puts them in the hardest diagnostic category.

A filter not enforced server side is a suggestion. When the filter carries a **tenant or permission predicate** it must be applied by the server from the authenticated identity, because a caller-supplied tenant filter is an authorization bypass with extra steps.

### Versioning and deprecation

Three placements, with different blast radii.

| Strategy | Form | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **URI** | `/v2/contracts` | Most visible, easiest to route and cache, hardest to run two versions of one resource. Encourages large infrequent version bumps |
| **Header** | `API-Version: 2026-03-01` | Invisible in logs unless you log it, easy to default wrongly, allows fine-grained dated versions |
| **Media type** | `Accept: application/vnd.acme.contract.v2+json` | Formally correct, poorly supported by tooling and by most client code, rarely worth the friction |

**Decision rule: use URI versioning for the coarse contract and dated header versioning for behavioral changes within it, and never ship a version without shipping the deprecation policy at the same time.**

The deprecation policy is the part that gets skipped and the part that costs money. Five elements, and a policy missing any one is not a policy.

1. **A stated support window** per version, as a duration, not "until we decide".
2. **A deprecation signal in the response itself**, so consumers discover it from traffic rather than from an email nobody read.
3. **A published migration path** enumerating the breaking changes, not a changelog.
4. **Usage telemetry per version per consumer**, because the whole point is being able to say who is still on the old version.
5. **A sunset mechanism that has been rehearsed** at least once outside production.

The AI-specific addition: **the prompt is a consumer of the API contract.** A tool description or few-shot example that embeds the shape of a v1 response breaks when v1 goes, and prompts appear in no package manager's dependency graph. Pinning a model and pinning an API are one discipline applied to two dependencies.

### Rate limits and quota design

Rate limits exist in three layers and confusing them produces the wrong remedy.

| Layer | Enforced by | Exceeded means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Provider limits** | The model provider, typically on requests per minute and tokens per minute, often separately for input and output | Your organization as a whole is over the ceiling. The remedy is scheduling and tiering, not client retries |
| **Gateway limits** | Your own gateway, per tenant, per application, per user | One consumer is taking capacity from another. The remedy is quota policy |
| **Downstream limits** | The tool's backing system, which the model has no awareness of | An agent fan-out has become a denial of service against your own customer relationship management system. The remedy is concurrency limits at the tool layer |

The third is the one architects miss. A model calling a search tool in a loop can generate more load against an internal system in a minute than the whole human user population generates in a day, and its owner will discover this in an incident. **Every tool that calls an internal system needs its own concurrency ceiling, independent of the model's rate limit.**

Quota design specifies four things: the unit (requests, tokens or currency), the window, the burst allowance and the behavior at the limit (reject, queue or degrade). **Decision rule: quota in the unit the cost is incurred in, which for models is tokens or currency, because a request is not a unit of anything.**

### Size limits against context limits

Two ceilings interact and neither is aware of the other.

| Ceiling | Set by | Symptom when hit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Request and response body limits** | The API, the gateway, the load balancer and often a proxy nobody remembers | 413, a truncated body or a connection reset. Frequently the proxy limit is the binding one and is lower than the documented API limit |
| **Context window** | The model | Silent degradation or an explicit error, depending on where truncation happens |

The interaction: a tool with no result cap will eventually return something that fits the HTTP layer and destroys the context. The fix is a **result contract**: every tool declares a maximum result size, truncates deterministically and says in the payload that truncation occurred and how to get the rest. A tool that truncates silently teaches the model it has seen everything.

**Decision rule: every tool result is bounded, the bound is declared in the tool description, and truncation is always visible in the payload.**

---

## 3.4 JSON and schema discipline

### The schema is the contract

**JSON Schema** is the only artifact in an AI integration that both a human reviewer and a runtime validator can hold. It is the tool input contract, the structured output contract, the documentation and, done properly, the governance surface. Treating it as generated boilerplate is how silent data defects enter.

The property most schemas omit is `additionalProperties: false`. Without it an object accepts any field it does not know about, so a model that invents a field gets no feedback, the field is dropped downstream and the record is wrong with no error anywhere. **Loose schemas do not produce errors. They produce quiet, plausible, wrong data,** invisible to monitoring and findable only by evaluation or human review.

### Additive versus breaking

| Change | Class | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add an optional field | **Additive** | Old consumers ignore it |
| Add a required field | **Breaking** | Old producers fail validation |
| Remove a field | **Breaking** for consumers reading it | Even if nothing writes it |
| Widen an enum | **Breaking for consumers**, additive for producers | A consumer with an exhaustive switch now has an unhandled case |
| Narrow an enum | **Breaking for producers** | A previously valid value is now rejected |
| Loosen a type, for example string to string-or-number | **Breaking** in practice | Every consumer's parsing assumption changes |
| Tighten a constraint, for example a new max length | **Breaking** | Existing valid data becomes invalid |
| Change a field from nullable to non-nullable | **Breaking** | Historical records fail |

**Decision rule: additive means old producers and old consumers both keep working unchanged, and if you have to check which side breaks, it is breaking.**

**Nullability** is the most abused part of any schema. Three distinct states get collapsed into one: **absent** (never captured), **null** (captured as having no value) and **empty** (zero, empty string, empty list). In a corpus, "no effective date recorded" and "effective date not applicable" are different facts with different governance consequences, and modeling both as `null` destroys information at ingest that nothing downstream can recover.

The AI-specific consequence: **a required field with no legitimate value forces the model to invent one.** An author who marks every field required to "get complete data" has built a hallucination generator. Required means the caller must always be able to know it. Optional means it might legitimately not.

### Enums as a governance surface

An enum is not a convenience. It is the point at which a business's controlled vocabulary becomes machine-enforced. Four consequences.

1. **An enum is an allowlist.** A `risk_level` field typed as a free string permits any value the model produces. Typed as an enum of four values, it cannot produce a fifth.
2. **Enum changes are policy changes.** Adding `escalate_to_legal` to an action enum expands what the system can do, and that expansion should go through the same review as adding a tool.
3. **Enums must be documented in the schema**, using `description` per value where the runtime supports it, because the model selects from an enum by reading its names and a badly named value is selected badly.
4. **Enums need an explicit "other" or "unknown" member where reality has one**, or the model will map every unmatched case onto the nearest available value and the distribution of that value becomes meaningless.

### A wrong tool input schema and its correction

The wrong version, which passes review because it looks tidy.

```json
{
  "name": "create_refund",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "customer": { "type": "string" },
      "amount": { "type": "number" },
      "reason": { "type": "string" },
      "approved_by": { "type": "string" }
    },
    "required": ["customer", "amount", "reason", "approved_by"]
  }
}
```

Six defects, and each is a separate production incident.

| Defect | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| `customer` is an untyped string | The model passes a name, an email or an internal identifier depending on what it saw. Resolution is ambiguous, and ambiguity resolves silently to the wrong customer |
| `amount` is an unconstrained number | Negative refunds, floating point currency, no ceiling. A model that misreads a total issues it |
| No currency field | The amount is meaningless in a multi-currency business and defaults to whatever the backend assumes |
| `reason` is free text where the business has a fixed set | Unanalyzable, and unenforceable against policy |
| `approved_by` is a required model-supplied field | **The worst defect.** The model is being asked to assert an authorization fact. It will produce a plausible name. Approval is now a hallucination with an audit trail |
| No `additionalProperties: false`, no idempotency key | Invented fields dropped silently, and retries duplicate refunds |

The corrected version.

```json
{
  "name": "create_refund",
  "description": "Request a refund on a settled order. Does not approve it; the refunds service approves against caller entitlements.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "properties": {
      "order_id":     {"type": "string", "pattern": "^ord_[0-9a-f]{16}$"},
      "amount_minor": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 500000},
      "currency":     {"type": "string", "enum": ["USD","EUR","GBP"]},
      "reason_code":  {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["damaged", "not_received",
                                "duplicate_charge",
                                "cancelled_in_window", "other"]},
      "reason_note":  {"type": "string", "maxLength": 500},
      "idempotency_key": {"type": "string", "format": "uuid"}
    },
    "required": ["order_id", "amount_minor", "currency",
                 "reason_code", "idempotency_key"]
  }
}
```

Five changes carry the weight. The customer is gone entirely, because the customer is derivable from the order and an agent should never be able to name the counterparty. Money is an integer in minor units with a bounded range and an explicit currency. The reason is an enum with a documented escape hatch and a separate free-text note that no logic depends on. The approver is gone, because **authorization is performed by the refunds service against the caller's identity and is not an input the model can supply.** And the description states what the tool does not do, which is the sentence that stops the model treating a request as an approval.

**Decision rule: if a field in a tool schema asserts a fact the model cannot know, remove the field and have the system supply it.**

### Schema registry practice

A **schema registry** is a versioned, addressable store of schemas with compatibility rules enforced at publish time. Four practices distinguish one that works.

| Practice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Compatibility mode declared per schema (backward, forward or full) and enforced on publish | Turns "we agreed not to break this" into a build failure |
| Schemas referenced by identifier from both producer and consumer, never copied | Copied schemas drift, and drift is discovered in production |
| Tool input schemas and structured output schemas registered alongside service schemas | They are contracts of the same kind and belong in the same inventory |
| Deprecation and ownership metadata on every schema | An unowned schema cannot be changed by anyone and is therefore permanent |

---

## 3.5 Authentication and authorization

Authentication establishes who someone is. Authorization determines what they may do. Most real gaps sit in the second.

### The flows, and when each is correct

| Flow | Who holds the credential | Correct when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Authorization code with PKCE** | The end user, at the identity provider. The client never holds a long-lived secret | A human is present and the application acts with that human's entitlements. PKCE is now the default even for confidential clients, not an alternative for mobile |
| **Client credentials** | The service itself | A backend acts as itself, with no user in the picture. Nightly batch, index refresh, system-to-system |
| **On-behalf-of / token exchange** | Service A holds a user token and needs a token for service B | A chain of services must preserve the user's identity rather than collapse to a service identity. The mechanism that prevents the shared privileged service account |
| **Device authorization** | The user, on a second device | A command line tool or a device with no browser |
| **Workload identity** | The platform, attested from the runtime | A workload proves what it is (this pod, this service account, this cloud role) without a stored secret. The strongest machine identity available |
| **mTLS** | Both sides, as certificates | Network-level mutual proof between services, often as a second factor beneath a token rather than instead of one |
| **API key** | Whoever has the string | Nothing, strictly. In practice: low-risk read paths, partner onboarding and any system that cannot do better |

**Decision rule: use the flow that carries the smallest identity sufficient to authorize the action, and prefer any mechanism that produces a short-lived credential over any mechanism that produces a stored one.**

**Why API keys persist** is worth stating honestly, because an architect who simply forbids them will be ignored. They work in every client, need no redirect, clock, discovery document or library; partner integrations are negotiated by people who cannot run an identity project; and rotation is a business conversation rather than a technical one. The response is not prohibition but **containment**: scoped to one capability, bound to a source network range where possible, issued per consumer so revocation is surgical, held in a secrets manager, rotated on a rehearsed schedule and never sufficient alone for a state-changing operation on regulated data.

### JWT validation mistakes

A **JSON Web Token** is only as good as its validation, and validation is done wrong in a small number of recurring ways.

| Mistake | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Decoding without verifying the signature | Anyone can mint any identity. The decode function and the verify function have similar names in most libraries and this is not an accident of history that anyone finds funny |
| Trusting the `alg` header | The classic `none` and the symmetric-key confusion attack. Pin the expected algorithm server side and ignore the token's claim about itself |
| Not validating `iss` and `aud` | A token minted by the right provider for a different application is accepted. This is a real and common cross-tenant path |
| Not validating `exp` and `nbf` with bounded clock skew | Expired tokens accepted indefinitely |
| Fetching signing keys without caching, or caching without honoring rotation | Either a denial of service against the provider or an outage at every key rotation |
| Treating the token as an authorization decision | The token says who. It does not say may. Entitlements are evaluated at the resource, at the time of the action |
| Putting sensitive data in claims | A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Its contents are readable by anything it passes through, including your logs |

### Scopes, roles and attributes

Three models, layered rather than alternative.

| Model | Grants | Right question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scope** | What an application may ask for on a user's behalf | "Was this capability consented to for this client?" |
| **Role** | What a class of principal may do | "Does this kind of user do this kind of thing?" |
| **Attribute** | What this principal may do to this object in this context | "Does this user have this relationship to this record, right now?" |

The layering is strict and each layer is necessary. **Scope bounds the application. Role bounds the person. Attribute bounds the record.** A design that stops at scopes authorizes the app and not the user. A design that stops at roles authorizes the user and not the row, which is exactly the failure that produces cross-matter and cross-tenant disclosure in retrieval systems.

**Decision rule: scope at the client, role at the principal, attribute at the object, and the effective permission is the intersection of all three with the task's requirement.**

### Who is acting: the four cases

The question every access decision in an agentic system must answer explicitly, because getting it implicit is where privilege escalation lives.

| Case | Identity presented downstream | Authorization basis | Failure mode when done wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **User acting directly** | The user's own token | The user's entitlements | Rare and well understood |
| **Agent acting for a user** | The user's identity, carried by token exchange, with an agent marker in the token or request | **Intersection** of what the user may do and what the task requires. Never the union, never the user's full set | The agent inherits everything the user can do, so a scheduling agent can read payroll because its principal can |
| **Agent acting for the system** | A workload identity for that specific agent, not a shared service account | The narrow set the automated function requires, defined as a role that no human holds | One privileged service account for all integrations, which makes every log line say the same thing and every entitlement question unanswerable |
| **Agent acting for another agent** | Delegated identity with a **recorded chain**, each hop attenuating and never expanding | The intersection of every principal in the chain with the current task's requirement | Privilege laundering: agent A cannot do X, calls agent B which can, and the audit trail shows B acting alone |

Two supporting rules make the table operational.

**Attenuation only.** A delegation may reduce the permission set and may never enlarge it. Any hop where the callee's effective permission exceeds the caller's is a defect regardless of how it was configured.

**The chain is recorded and is queryable.** "Which human caused this action" must be answerable from a single record, not reconstructed by joining logs from four services. If the chain is not in the token or in a correlated trace, it does not exist.

### The confused deputy

The **confused deputy problem** is a privileged component performing an action on behalf of a less privileged caller, using its own authority rather than the caller's. It is the structural description of most agent authorization failures and it has three manifestations in this domain.

| Manifestation | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| **Service account deputy** | The integration authenticates as itself and passes the user's request through, so every user has the integration's permissions |
| **Retrieval deputy** | The index was built by a privileged crawler, so the index contains everything, and permission filtering at query time is the only thing standing between a user and content they may not see. If the filter is applied after similarity ranking, or forgotten in one code path, disclosure follows |
| **Injection deputy** | Content the agent reads contains instructions. The agent has authority. The content does not, but the agent cannot tell the difference and acts with its own privilege on the content's behalf. This is the confused deputy with the attacker supplying the confusion |

⧉ **The single largest risk in this part: an agent that holds a privileged identity and reads untrusted content is a confused deputy by construction, and no prompt-level mitigation changes that.** The structural controls are the only ones that count: the agent carries the user's attenuated identity rather than a privileged one; untrusted content arrives as tool results and never as instructions; every consequential action is authorized in code against the caller's entitlements at the moment of execution; and irreversible actions pass a gate that content cannot influence. An architecture that relies on the model declining to follow injected instructions has placed the security boundary inside the model.

### Secrets, rotation and short-lived credentials

| Property | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **Storage** | A secrets manager or platform-native workload identity. Never in source, never in a container image, never in a configuration file that is shared to make onboarding easier |
| **Injection** | Referenced by name at runtime, resolved by the platform, so the configuration artifact is shareable and the secret is not |
| **Lifetime** | Minutes to hours. The correct number of long-lived credentials in a modern architecture is as close to zero as the legacy estate permits |
| **Rotation** | Automated, scheduled and **rehearsed**. An unrehearsed rotation path is an outage waiting for a compromise to trigger it |
| **Revocation** | Tested. "We would rotate the key" is not a control until someone has done it under time pressure |
| **Blast radius** | One credential per consumer per capability, so revocation is surgical rather than an incident of its own |
| **Logging** | Secrets are never logged, and the redaction that guarantees this is applied at the logging library, not left to each call site |

### The gaps in practice

The recurring authorization gaps, what each looks like and the fix.

| Gap | What it looks like | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Shared privileged service account** | The integration authenticates as one identity that can do everything any user might need | Carry end-user identity through to the backend; let the backend enforce that user's entitlements |
| **Agent inherits full operator scope** | An agent acting for a user holds everything the user may do | Grant the intersection of what the user may do and what the task requires |
| **Model asked to enforce authorization** | The prompt says "only issue refunds for verified customers" | **Authorization belongs outside the model, in code, before the action executes.** The model may request; the system decides |
| **Credentials in shared configuration** | Secrets in a committed file, shared across a team or logged | Environment-variable expansion or a secrets manager, so configuration can be shared without sharing credentials |
| **Long-lived credentials** | No expiry, no rotation, no tested revocation path | Short-lived tokens and a revocation mechanism you have actually exercised |
| **No per-request attribution** | Logs cannot answer "who caused this action" | Identity captured per request. ⚠ Where protected health information is in scope this maps to the HIPAA audit-controls expectation, but whether a given logging design satisfies it is a determination for the compliance function rather than the architecture team |
| **Tenant bleed in retrieval** | Similarity search crosses organizational boundaries | Permission and tenant filters applied **before** similarity, never after |
| **Injected instruction treated as authority** | Content the system reads changes what it does | Treat all fetched content as data. Deliver it in tool results. Gate consequential actions behind checks content cannot influence. See 4.4 |
| **Over-broad scope at the connector** | The connected service exposes everything it can do | Scope at the server as well as at the agent |

**The principle: the model is not a security boundary.** Boundaries are enforced by the systems around it. A design that makes the model responsible for a security decision is wrong.

### Protocol-level authorization: MCP and agent-to-agent

3.1 chooses the integration mechanism. This is the authorization model that comes with the choice, and it is where the gaps above become concrete because the protocol decides what a token means.

**A remote MCP server is a resource server, not a proxy.** The correct shape is the standard delegated-authorization one: the client discovers the server's authorization server, obtains a token scoped to that specific server, and presents it on each call. Three properties make the difference between that shape and something that merely resembles it.

| Property | What it requires | What goes wrong without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Audience binding** | The token names the specific MCP server it is valid for, and the server rejects a token issued for anything else | A token obtained for one server is replayable against another that trusts the same issuer, which converts a low-value connector into an entry point to a high-value one |
| **Dynamic or governed client registration** | Clients are registered, either automatically through the protocol's registration flow or explicitly by the platform team, so every client is identifiable and revocable | An unenumerable client population. Revocation becomes a broadcast rather than a surgical act, and nobody can answer which clients hold access |
| **No token passthrough** | The MCP server does not accept a token issued for a downstream service and forward it. It obtains its own credential for the downstream call | The downstream service sees only the MCP server's traffic with a token it trusts, the audience check it would have performed is bypassed, and the confused deputy of 3.5 reappears one layer down |

⧉ **Token passthrough is the anti-pattern that looks like an optimization.** Forwarding the caller's downstream token removes a credential exchange and appears to preserve end-user identity. What it actually does is delete the boundary between the connector and the system behind it, so a scope granted for the connector becomes a scope held against everything the connector can reach. Carry identity as a claim, not as a reusable credential for someone else's service.

**Local versus remote is an authorization decision before it is a deployment decision.** A local MCP server runs with the desktop user's ambient authority: their filesystem, their network position, their already-authenticated sessions. Nothing in the protocol constrains that, and no central function can see it. This is why 3.1's rule holds. Anything that reads or changes regulated data is a remote server behind the gateway, where the token, the scope, the audience and the log are all things the organization controls.

**Agent-to-agent adds two questions the single-agent case never raises.** First, on whose behalf is the calling agent acting, and does the receiving agent get to know? An agent card that declares authentication requirements has stated how to authenticate the calling *agent*, which is not the same as establishing the human principal behind the request. Where the receiving side's authorization depends on the human, the human's identity must travel as a verifiable claim and be checked, not asserted in a message field. Second, how far does delegation extend? Authority should attenuate at every hop and never widen, and the chain should be recorded, so that an action three agents deep can be traced back to the grant that permitted it. ⚠ Cross-organizational agent-to-agent interaction adds a liability question that architecture does not settle: whose act is it when an agent operated by one party instructs an agent operated by another. Put it to counsel before the integration ships, not after it fails.

---

## 3.6 Webhooks and event-driven integration

### Push versus pull

| | Pull (polling) | Push (webhook or event) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency | Bounded by the interval | Near immediate |
| Load | Constant, mostly wasted | Proportional to actual events |
| Failure handling | Trivial. The next poll catches up | Requires retries, dead lettering and idempotency on the receiver |
| Receiver requirements | None. The receiver initiates | A reachable, authenticated, always-available endpoint |
| Ordering | Whatever the query returns | Not guaranteed |

**Decision rule: poll when the volume is low and the receiver is unreliable, push when latency matters or the event rate is high enough that polling is mostly empty, and expect to build both because push needs a reconciliation poll to catch what it dropped.**

That last clause is the part designs omit. **Every push integration needs a periodic reconciliation sweep**, because at-least-once delivery is a promise about retries and not a promise about correctness, and the day the dead letter queue overflows is the day the sweep is the only thing that repairs state.

### Webhook security

Four requirements, and a webhook receiver missing any one is exploitable.

1. **Signature verification** over the **raw bytes before any parsing**, compared in constant time. Verifying after deserialization and re-serialization is the standard way this is implemented wrongly, because the byte sequence changes.
2. **Timestamp binding and replay protection.** The signature covers a timestamp, anything outside a small window is rejected, and recently seen message identifiers are retained for at least that window.
3. **Transport and network controls.** Mutual transport layer security or source address restriction, so the signing secret is not the only barrier.
4. **Independent authorization.** A webhook says an event happened, not what the receiver may do about it. It is untrusted input with a signature, not an instruction.

### Delivery semantics

**At-least-once** is what real systems deliver. Exactly-once is a property of a system boundary, not of a network, and it is achieved by making the receiver idempotent rather than by making the sender careful.

| Concern | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Duplicates | An event identifier the receiver records before acting, with the same before-not-after ordering as idempotency keys |
| Ordering | A per-key sequence number or version, with the receiver discarding anything older than what it has already applied. Global ordering is expensive and almost never required. **Per-entity ordering is the requirement that actually exists** |
| Poison messages | A **dead letter queue** with a retry ceiling, alerting on depth and, critically, a documented and rehearsed replay procedure. A dead letter queue nobody drains is a data loss mechanism with good intentions |
| Backpressure | Bounded queues and consumer-driven pull rather than unbounded buffering. The failure mode of unbounded buffering is that latency grows until the system is useless while every health check stays green |
| Dual write | The **outbox pattern**: the state change and the outbound event are written in one local transaction to the same database, and a separate relay publishes from the outbox. This removes the window in which the database commits and the publish fails, which is the single most common source of enterprise data divergence |

### Event bus versus direct call

| Choose direct call when | Choose event bus when |
| --- | --- |
| The caller needs the result to continue | The producer does not care who consumes |
| There is exactly one consumer and it is known | Consumers are added over time without changing the producer |
| The operation is synchronous by nature | The work is fire and forget or fan-out |
| Failure should be the caller's problem | Failure should be retried independently of the producer |

**Decision rule: use an event bus when the number of consumers is expected to change and direct calls when the caller needs the answer, and never introduce a bus to decouple two systems that will always be exactly two systems.**

### Long-running agent work in a request-response world

The structural mismatch: enterprise integration assumes a call returns in milliseconds to seconds, and an agent run takes seconds to hours. Three shapes resolve it, and they are not alternatives so much as a progression by duration.

```
 SYNC PATH  (sub-second to a few seconds)
   client --request--> gateway --> model --> response --> client

 STREAM PATH  (a user is waiting, output is long)
   client --request--> gateway --> model
       <-- token stream ------------   |
       <-- final message + usage ---   |

 ASYNC PATH  (agent run, minutes to hours)
   client --POST /runs--------> api --> queue --> worker --> tools
       <-- 202 Accepted, run_id --                  |
   client --GET /runs/{id}----> api            (checkpoints
       <-- running | needs_input | done --       persisted)
   api ----signed webhook----> client callback <---+
```

| Shape | Use when | Must also provide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synchronous** | The work reliably finishes inside the client's timeout, with headroom | A timeout shorter than every upstream timeout in the chain |
| **Streaming** | A human is waiting and partial output is useful | A defined behavior for a stream that dies mid-response, and accounting for the fact that a streamed partial answer may already have been read by the user |
| **Asynchronous job plus callback** | The work may exceed any reasonable request timeout, or must survive a client disconnect | A durable run record, a polling endpoint as well as the callback, a `needs_input` state for human gates and cancellation |

Three details separate a working async design from a broken one. **A run identifier issued before the work starts**, so a client that loses its connection can recover. **A polling endpoint in addition to the callback**, because callbacks fail and the client must not be dependent on the thing most likely to break. And **a terminal state for every run**, including canceled, expired and failed, because a run stuck in `running` forever is indistinguishable from a run that is genuinely slow and the operations team will treat both the same way, which is to say badly.

**Decision rule: if the work can exceed thirty seconds, design it as a job with an identifier from the start, because retrofitting asynchrony onto a synchronous contract requires changing every caller.**

---

## 3.7 Middleware and the AI gateway

An **AI gateway** is the single control point through which all model traffic in an enterprise passes. Arguing for it as plumbing loses the argument. Arguing for it as a governance, risk management and compliance control point wins it, because everything a compliance function needs to assert about model use is either implemented at the gateway or implemented eleven times inconsistently in eleven applications.

```
 CALLERS            AI GATEWAY                       PROVIDERS
 +--------+   +-----------------------------+   +--------------+
 | app A  |-->| 1 authn + tenant resolve    |-->| model, cloud |
 | app B  |   | 2 policy + classification   |   +--------------+
 | agent  |   | 3 redaction inbound         |
 +--------+   | 4 routing + model pin       |   +--------------+
              | 5 quota / rate / budget     |-->| model, in    |
              | 6 cache lookup              |   | private net  |
              | 7 call + retry + failover   |   +--------------+
              | 8 redaction out + filters   |
              | 9 log / trace / attribute   |   +--------------+
              +-----------------------------+-->| self-hosted  |
                     |            |             +--------------+
                 +-------+   +---------+
                 | audit |   | metrics |
                 | store |   | + evals |
                 +-------+   +---------+
```

| Function | What it is | Why it cannot live in the application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Routing** | Model and deployment selection by task class, data classification and tenant | Route policy is a governance decision and must change without redeploying eleven applications |
| **Key management** | Provider credentials held once, never distributed to callers | Distributed keys cannot be rotated or revoked without coordinated releases |
| **Quota and budget** | Per tenant, per application, per user, in tokens and currency | A per-application limit cannot see aggregate spend |
| **Caching** | Response cache and prompt cache orchestration | Cache hit ratio is an enterprise cost metric, not an application detail |
| **Prompt and response logging** | The complete record of what was sent and returned | It is the evidence base. Applications log inconsistently and delete on their own schedules |
| **Redaction** | Detection and masking of sensitive values in both directions | A control that must be uniform to be assertable |
| **Policy enforcement** | Classification checks, blocked categories, mandatory system content, tool allowlists | This is the actual control point. Policy in application code is policy nobody can inventory |
| **Fallback and failover** | Secondary model, secondary region, degraded mode | Availability engineering that no application should reimplement |
| **Cost attribution** | Every call tagged to a tenant, application, feature and business unit | Chargeback and unit economics are impossible retroactively |
| **Tenant isolation** | Enforced separation of keys, caches, logs and quotas per tenant | Cache and log bleed across tenants is a disclosure event |

Three failure modes of gateways worth pre-empting, because each turns the control point into a liability.

1. **Single point of failure.** Keep it stateless and horizontally scaled, with a governed bypass path. A gateway that adds an outage a quarter loses its mandate.
2. **Bottleneck for change.** If adding a model needs a gateway ticket with a multi-week lead time, teams route around it and the control evaporates. Policy must be data, and self-service must be real.
3. **A second place logic lives.** Prompt content and business rules leaking into the gateway produce a system nobody can reason about. It does identity, policy, routing, limits, redaction and observability. It does not do prompts.

**Decision rule: put a capability in the gateway when it must be uniform across all applications to be assertable to an auditor, and leave it in the application otherwise.**

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** Who is allowed not to use it. A control point everything is supposed to pass through is only a control point if the exceptions are enumerable, and the first production incident is the moment someone will ask for one.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Making the gateway the mandatory path for model traffic | Who may authorize a bypass, on what grounds and for how long | Bypass register with an expiry on every entry. Platform owner with the risk owner |
| Setting routing and policy by data classification | Which forum approves a policy change, given that it changes behavior in every application at once and without a release | Versioned policy set with an approval record. Architecture review board |
| Enforcing tenant isolation of keys, caches, logs and quotas | Whether the isolation is tested rather than asserted, since a cache or a log crossing tenants is a disclosure event | Isolation test evidence per release. Security architect |

The logging retention and access rows that also run through here belong to 8.5, and the budget ceiling and its lifting authority to 8.10. They are not repeated, because the artifact has one owner.

**What this costs the organization.** Centralizing the control centralizes the outage and the change queue with it. The cost people forget is that the bypass register and a real self-service path are the price of the mandate rather than concessions against it: a gateway teams route around has the liability of a control point and the assurance value of none.

**The executive translation.** Everything we would have to assert to an auditor about model use is asserted once here or eleven times inconsistently elsewhere, which makes this a compliance asset with an availability obligation attached to it.

---

## 3.8 Error handling and resilience

### The twelve failure classes

| Class | Detect by | Retry | Backoff | Fallback | Surface to user |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Transport** (connection reset, DNS, TLS) | Exception before any response | Yes | Exponential with jitter | Alternate endpoint or region | No, unless retries exhaust |
| **Authentication** (401) | Status | **Once**, after refresh | None | None | No. It is an operational fault |
| **Authorization** (403) | Status | **Never** | n/a | None | **Yes**, as a permission outcome, not an error |
| **Rate limit** (429) | Status and headers | Yes | Honor `Retry-After`, then exponential with jitter, plus reduce concurrency | Lower-tier model or queue | Only as a delay, not as an error |
| **Overload** (529) | Status | Yes | Exponential with jitter, longer ceiling | **Yes**, secondary provider or region | No, if fallback succeeds |
| **Timeout** | Elapsed time at the caller | **Only if idempotent** | Yes | Degrade to a shorter or simpler call | If it exhausts |
| **Malformed output** (unparseable, schema violation) | Validation against the schema | Yes, with the validation error returned to the model, **bounded to two or three attempts** | None needed | Simpler schema, or deterministic extraction | Only after the bound |
| **Refusal** | Stop reason and content inspection | **No** as-is. A retry of the same prompt is not a strategy | n/a | Re-route to a human or a different framing that is itself reviewed | **Yes**, honestly. A refusal presented as a system error trains users to retry until it complies |
| **Hallucinated tool call** (nonexistent tool, invented arguments) | Dispatch table lookup fails, or validation fails | Yes, with an explicit error result naming the available tools | None | Reduce catalog size, improve descriptions | No |
| **Tool execution failure** (the tool ran and failed) | Tool result carries an error | **Depends on the tool's idempotency** | Per tool | Alternate tool or degraded answer | Depends on stakes |
| **Downstream failure** (the tool's backing system is down) | Error class from the tool | Bounded, then stop | Yes | Cached data with a staleness marker, or a stated inability | **Yes**, as reduced capability, not as a wrong answer |
| **Partial success** (some of a fan-out succeeded) | Result aggregation | Retry only the failed units | Per unit | Return what succeeded, **explicitly marked as partial** | **Yes**. A partial result presented as complete is the worst outcome in this table |

**Decision rule: retry only what a retry can fix, and a retry can fix transport, capacity and shape, never permission, policy or semantics.**

Two rows carry extra weight. **Refusal is not an error class to be engineered around.** A rising refusal rate is a configuration signal and over-restriction is a defect, but the remedy sits in the design review, not in a loop that varies the prompt until the model complies. And **partial success is the class most often unhandled**, because the happy path and the total failure path both get written and the middle does not. An agent that called five tools, had two fail and synthesized the other three confidently has produced a wrong answer with full internal consistency.

### Resilience mechanisms

| Mechanism | What it does | The mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Exponential backoff with jitter** | Spreads retries so a recovering service is not immediately re-flooded | Backoff without jitter. Synchronized clients retry in lockstep and produce a thundering herd that re-downs the service that just recovered |
| **Retry budget** | Caps retries as a fraction of total traffic, for example a low single-digit percentage | Per-request retry limits with no global cap. Each caller is polite and the aggregate is a denial of service |
| **Circuit breaker** | Opens after a failure threshold, fails fast while open, allows trial requests when half open | No half-open state, so it never closes; or a breaker per process, so a hundred processes each independently discover the outage |
| **Bulkhead** | Isolates resource pools per dependency so one slow dependency cannot consume all connections or threads | A single shared pool, so a slow document management system takes down the unrelated ticketing path |
| **Timeout at every layer** | Each layer's timeout is strictly shorter than its caller's | Inverted timeouts, where the inner call outlives the outer, so work continues after the client has given up and the user retries into an already-loaded system |
| **Graceful degradation** | A defined reduced-function mode: cached retrieval, smaller model, deterministic path or an honest inability | Undefined degradation, meaning the system degrades in whatever way the code happens to |
| **Hedged request** | A second request after a delay, taking the first response | Hedging non-idempotent work, which is duplication with a stopwatch |

The timeout rule is worth stating as a formula because it is violated constantly: **client timeout > gateway timeout > provider call timeout > tool timeout,** with meaningful gaps at each step, and every one of them shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout.

#### Where each control sits, and what a misplacement costs

The mechanisms above are usually specified without a location, and a control at the wrong layer protects a part of the system that was not at risk while leaving the part that was.

| Control | The layer it belongs at | What it is protecting against there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Retry with backoff** | Closest to the model call | A single transient response: a rate limit, a timeout, an overload. The failure is one request deep and the recovery is one request deep |
| **Circuit breaker** | The service boundary | A dependency that is degraded rather than momentarily unavailable. The breaker's job is to stop the calling system spending its own capacity waiting on something already known to be failing |
| **Fallback chain** | The orchestration layer | The absence of a usable answer from the primary path. Only the orchestrator knows what an acceptable substitute is: a lower tier, a cached response, a deterministic path, a degraded mode |

**The misplacements have distinct signatures.** A circuit breaker placed at the call site opens per process, so a hundred processes each discover the outage independently and none of them shortens anyone else's wait. A fallback implemented next to the API call cannot degrade the *task*, only the call, so it substitutes a model and returns an answer the workflow was not designed to accept. And retry logic hoisted into the orchestration layer retries the whole unit of work rather than the failed call, which multiplies cost and, on any non-idempotent step, is the duplication failure treated below.

**Fallback behavior belongs in the eval suite.** It is the control most often built and least often exercised, because the condition that triggers it does not occur during development. A fallback path that has never been scored is an assumption about what the system does under load, and the first time it runs will be the first time anyone sees its output.

### Never retry a non-idempotent action blindly

The rule has a stronger form for agents. **An agent's tool call that changed external state and then timed out is in an unknown state, and the correct response is to query, not to retry.** Three steps, in order.

1. **Determine what actually happened.** A read that establishes whether the effect occurred. This requires that the write path leave a queryable trace with the idempotency key on it.
2. **If it did not happen, retry with the same idempotency key.** Not a new one, which would defeat the mechanism.
3. **If it did happen, do not repeat it,** and make the fact that it happened visible in the run record so the agent does not decide to do it again on its own reasoning.

**Compensating transactions** are the remedy for the case where the action fired and should not have. Four requirements for a compensating action to be real.

| Requirement | Why |
| --- | --- |
| It exists as a first-class operation, designed with the forward operation | Compensation invented during an incident is unreviewed code in production |
| It is idempotent | It will itself be retried |
| It is authorized separately | The authority to send is not the authority to unsend |
| It is recorded as a distinct event, not as a deletion | Deleting the forward record destroys the audit trail of the very thing being corrected |

And the constraint that governs the design above it: **some actions have no compensation.** An email sent, a payment settled, a filing submitted, a message posted to a regulator. Those are the actions that must be behind a human gate, and the presence or absence of a compensating transaction is the sharpest available test for where gates belong.

---

## 3.9 Observability

### Three signals plus a fourth

| Signal | Answers | Consumer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Metrics** | Is it up, fast and within budget | Operations |
| **Logs** | What happened in this one request | Engineering |
| **Traces** | Where did the time and the control flow go across services | Engineering and architecture |
| **Evaluations** | **Was it right** | Product, risk and the business |

The fourth is the one that does not exist in ordinary systems and is the only one that detects the dominant AI failure mode. A fluent, well-formatted, confidently wrong answer produces a 200, a normal latency, a clean trace and a satisfied metric. **Metrics, logs and traces observe the machine. Only evaluation observes the answer.**

### What a trace of an agent run must contain

| Field | Why it is not optional |
| --- | --- |
| **Request identifier** | The unit of one call |
| **Session and conversation identifier** | The unit of one user's continuous work |
| **Run identifier** | The unit of one agent execution, spanning many model calls |
| **User and tenant identifier** | Attribution, entitlement questions and the ability to answer "who caused this" |
| **Model identifier and version, with effort or thinking configuration** | The first thing you want when quality moves, and the most commonly absent |
| **Prompt template identifier and version, or a hash of the rendered prompt** | Distinguishes a prompt change from a model change. A hash is the cheap version and it works |
| **Retrieval detail**: query, index and version, candidate identifiers with scores, what survived filtering, what was actually passed | Retrieval quality is invisible in the output and this is the only place it exists |
| **Tool calls**: name, arguments, result status, duration, error class and the idempotency key where present | What the system actually did, as opposed to what it said |
| **Token counts**, separated into input, cache write and cache read | They bill differently, and the split is the cache diagnostic |
| **Latency by segment**: time to first token, model time, tool time, retrieval time, queue time | An aggregate latency number cannot be acted on |
| **Stop reason** | Distinguishes completion from truncation from refusal from a tool-use pause |
| **Evaluation scores** attached to the run where available | Ties quality back to the specific configuration that produced it |
| **Human decisions**: approvals, rejections, edits and overrides, with the identity and timestamp | The cheapest labeled data available and the record a regulator asks for |
| **Cost**, per call and per completed outcome | The second number is the one that matters |

**Decision rule: if you cannot reconstruct a disputed answer from the trace alone, without access to production data as it stands today, the trace is incomplete.**

### Redaction, privilege and retention

Logs of an AI system contain the inputs and outputs, which means they contain whatever the users put in, which in an enterprise means regulated personal data, confidential business information and, in legal contexts, privileged material. Four consequences.

1. **Redaction happens on the write path**, in shared infrastructure. Redaction applied at query time means the sensitive data is already on disk.
2. **Log access is an entitlement**, granted narrowly and itself logged. A support engineer with open access to prompt logs has more reach than most database administrators.
3. **⚠ Privilege is not preserved by accident.** Where an AI system processes material that may be legally privileged, log content can become discoverable and privilege determinations are jurisdiction-specific and fact-specific. Design so that content logging can be disabled or segregated per workload, and confirm the handling requirements with counsel.
4. **Retention differs by purpose**, which is the point of the next table.

### Monitoring, evaluation and audit are three systems

Collapsing them is the most common observability design error, because they have different consumers, different retention and different access rules.

| | Monitoring | Evaluation | Audit log |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Question** | Is it working | Is it right | What happened and who is accountable |
| **Consumer** | Operations, on call | Product, quality, risk | Compliance, legal, regulators, litigation |
| **Latency** | Seconds | Batch, or per release | Written synchronously with the action |
| **Content** | Aggregates, mostly no payload | Sampled payloads with labels | Identity, action, target, decision, time, authority |
| **Retention** | Short, weeks to months | Medium, tied to model and prompt versions | **Long, set by regulation and legal hold, not by engineering** |
| **Mutability** | Freely mutable | Versioned | **Append only, tamper evident** |
| **Sampling** | Aggregated, so sampling is fine | Stratified sampling is correct and necessary | **None. Complete or it is not an audit log** |

**Decision rule: if a record could be evidence, it belongs in the audit log with audit retention and audit immutability, and putting it only in the application log means it will be gone before it is needed.**

### Sampling

Sample the successes and keep everything else. Four rules.

1. **Keep every error and every refusal**, in full.
2. **Keep every human override**, in full. It is the highest-value data in the system.
3. **Stratify the sample of successes** by segment, document type, tenant and confidence band, so that rare categories are represented rather than drowned. Uniform random sampling of a skewed population tells you about the majority case you already understand.
4. **Sample the high-confidence population deliberately.** It is the population nobody checks and therefore where a new failure mode survives longest.

### Correlating a business outcome back to a run

The business asks "did this work", and it is usually unanswerable because the identifier chain breaks between the agent run and the business event. The fix is that the run identifier is **written into the business record** at the moment of the action, not merely logged alongside it. The refund row carries the run that requested it. The ticket carries the run that drafted it.

**Decision rule: the run identifier belongs in the business system's row, not only in the observability platform, because observability data is retained for weeks and the business question is asked after quarters.**

### The four records, and observability as the precondition for autonomy

**A model-based system is harder to debug than a conventional one because it does not crash when it goes wrong. It produces a subtly wrong response.** Standard logging catches errors and timeouts. It does not catch a response that is quietly incorrect in a way that has business consequences, which is the failure this layer exists for.

Four records, on every request.

| Record | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| **The request** | Model version, input token count, prompt identifier |
| **The response** | Output token count, latency, stop reason |
| **The context** | User role, session identifier, whether caching was applied |
| **The outcome** | Whether the downstream system accepted the output, and any rejection signal it returned |

**The fourth is the one most often missing and the only one that closes the loop.** The first three describe what the system did. The outcome record describes whether it was any use, and without it the operational picture stops at the API boundary while the failure continues downstream.

**Security organizations increasingly treat observability as the precondition for enabling agents at all**, on the reasoning that an autonomous system without a trustworthy audit trail is not approvable to act. That converts observability from an operational nicety into an entry condition, and it belongs in the design review as a checklist item rather than in the operations backlog: verify which agentic actions are recorded in the audit logs on each surface the deployment uses. **Coverage varies by surface, and an action that is taken but not logged is, to a security reviewer, an action that cannot be allowed.**

⧉ **A shared API key across tenants destroys attribution at exactly the moment attribution is needed.** When an organization-level rate limit trips at peak load, the spike is visible and the tenant that caused it is not, and every tenant absorbs the impact. Separate keys per tenant are the instrument for attribution and isolation in any multi-tenant production deployment.
